title: Amritsar 1919
subtitle: The Day an Empire Shot at Its Own Shadow
era: Jallianwala Bagh massacre and Rowlatt protests, 1919
moral: Rule by terror destroys its own claim to legitimacy.

sources.citation: Report of the Disorders Inquiry Committee, the Hunter Committee Report (Government of India, 1920)
sources.note: Official inquiry including Dyer's testimony and casualty figures.

sources.citation: Rabindranath Tagore, letter to Viceroy Chelmsford returning his knighthood, 31 May 1919
sources.note: Primary Indian elite response to the massacre.

sources.citation: Kim A. Wagner, Amritsar 1919: An Empire of Fear and the Making of a Massacre (Yale, 2019)
sources.note: Recent reconstruction from military and administrative records.

panels.shot: low-angle wide of Reginald Dyer silhouetted at the mouth of a narrow walled ground, soldiers behind him, a dense unseen crowd suggested by shadows within

dialogue.text: Amritsar, 13 April 1919: on a spring Baisakhi afternoon, Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer walked into Jallianwala Bagh and chose a doctrine of terror over law, shattering India’s faith in imperial reform.

panels.shot: montage wide, bird’s-eye over Punjab plains with smaller inset of wartime posters and a telegraph office

dialogue.text: The Great War had ended, but its shadow lay over Punjab. Heavy recruitment, grain requisitions and censorship had left the province tense, even as Indians waited for promised political reforms.

panels.shot: medium wide of an Indian newspaper stall in Amritsar, people crowding around, some holding leaflets

dialogue.text: Instead came the Rowlatt Act of 1919, allowing detention without trial. From Delhi to Amritsar, people read the news and saw not reward for loyalty, but an empire tightening its fist.

panels.shot: street-level wide of an Amritsar protest meeting, with Saifuddin Kitchlew and Satyapal on a raised platform in the distance

dialogue.text: In Amritsar, local leaders like Saifuddin Kitchlew and Dr. Satyapal called for peaceful protest. Hartals closed shops, meetings denounced the Act, and for a few days, defiance stayed non-violent.

panels.shot: tight, tense medium of a British official’s carriage moving through a crowd, with Indian police flanking

dialogue.text: On 10 April, the authorities lured Kitchlew and Satyapal to the Deputy Commissioner’s house, arrested them and secretly dispatched them from the city. The news broke like a slap across Amritsar.

panels.shot: chaotic wide of Amritsar streets with smoke rising, a crowd surging, a European building in the background

dialogue.text: The city convulsed. Anger spilled into attacks on banks, telegraph lines and European property; several Europeans were assaulted and killed. The protest, leaderless and furious, crossed the thin line to riot.

panels.shot: medium close-up of Reginald Dyer reading a telegram in his quarters at Jalandhar, lamplight harsh

dialogue.text: To this troubled district came Brigadier-General Reginald Dyer, commanding the Jalandhar Brigade. Telegrams spoke of murders, arson and 'rebellion'. He saw not a city in distress, but a province on the brink of revolt.

panels.shot: low-angle medium of Dyer mounting a vehicle with troops around, early morning light

dialogue.text: On 11 April, he moved to Amritsar to 'restore order'. His reports and later testimony show a man convinced he faced a second 1857, determined, in his words, to produce a 'moral effect' at once.

panels.shot: wide shot of Amritsar street with martial law notices, Dyer observing from horseback

dialogue.text: As days passed, he imposed curfews, banned gatherings, and read the city’s mood through his own fear. On the morning of 13 April, he issued a proclamation forbidding public meetings without his permission.

panels.shot: sun-drenched wide of Jallianwala Bagh from above, showing the irregular walled enclosure and surrounding houses, with a gathering crowd

dialogue.text: That afternoon, thousands drifted into Jallianwala Bagh, a rough open ground hemmed in by walls and houses. Some came for a political meeting, others for the Baisakhi fair; many never heard any proclamation.

panels.shot: ground-level wide inside the Bagh, people sitting, children playing, a few men speaking in the distance

dialogue.text: Witnesses recalled a crowd unarmed and unworried. There were peasants, artisans, traders, women with infants, youths curious about politics. The air held talk, not slogans; expectation, not war.

panels.shot: tense medium-wide at the narrow entrance to the Bagh, Dyer and column entering single file

dialogue.text: Then boots sounded in the lanes. Without giving prior warning inside the Bagh or attempting to disperse the meeting peacefully, Dyer marched in with about fifty troops, roughly half armed with rifles.

panels.shot: low-angle close on Dyer’s face as he surveys the crowd, his gaze hard, hand raised

dialogue.text: Later, before the Hunter Committee, he admitted he had come 'to teach a moral lesson' and had decided on firing in advance. In that paused moment, he chose exemplary terror over any lesser show of force.

panels.shot: wide shot from behind the firing line, rifles aimed into a packed crowd already beginning to panic

dialogue.text: Without ordering a warning shot or calling on the crowd to disperse, he gave the command. The rifles spoke again and again, the troops firing into the densest parts of the crowd until their ammunition nearly ran out.

panels.shot: high-angle wide of the interior of the Bagh during the firing, people scrambling, some climbing walls, others near the well

dialogue.text: Survivors spoke of panic in a trap: high walls, few exits, no shelter. Some tried to scale the sides, some ran for the narrow lanes, some leapt into the well. The firing lasted about ten minutes.

panels.shot: medium shot of Dyer signaling to stop, smoke hanging, soldiers lowering rifles

dialogue.text: They fired some 1,650 rounds. Officially, 379 were reported killed and about 1,200 wounded; Indian leaders and local committees put the dead far higher. Dyer stopped only when, by his account, 'the crowd was dispersing'.

panels.shot: medium-wide as Dyer turns away from the Bagh entrance, troops falling in behind him, leaving the ground

dialogue.text: He ordered no medical aid, imposed no curfew to help the injured, and left the wounded where they lay. He would later tell the inquiry that help arriving earlier would not, in his view, have altered matters.

panels.shot: somber wide of the Bagh at dusk, lanterns flickering as people search for loved ones among still forms

dialogue.text: Night fell on a ground of moans and unanswered names. Families ventured in at risk, carrying away the injured as best they could. There were no official lists, no prompt inquest, only rumours and grief.

panels.shot: stark medium of Dyer before a table of British officials, Hunter Committee style inquiry room

dialogue.text: The Hunter Committee later questioned him. Dyer calmly defended his action as necessary to prevent rebellion and stated he would have used machine guns if the lanes had allowed, insisting terror was his chosen instrument of control.

panels.shot: collage shot: one side Tagore writing at his desk, the other a London drawing room with Britons toasting Dyer

dialogue.text: Across India, outrage grew. Tagore returned his knighthood, calling it a badge of shame. Yet in Britain, many in the conservative press and the 'Morning Post' fund hailed Dyer as the 'Saviour of India'.

panels.shot: medium of Dyer leaving a military office, hat in hand, a clerk watching, expression unreadable

dialogue.text: The government could not wholly ignore the outcry. The Hunter Report condemned his conduct as inexcusable and 'a grave error', and he was relieved of his command and retired, though he faced no criminal trial.

panels.shot: street-level shot of Amritsar under martial measures: Indians crawling in a lane under soldier supervision

dialogue.text: In the days after, further punitive measures deepened humiliation. In one Amritsar lane, people were compelled to crawl as punishment for an assault on a missionary. Such scenes fixed the sense of a rule propped by fear.

panels.shot: present-day wide of the Jallianwala Bagh memorial, flame and names on a wall, visitors walking silently

dialogue.text: Today, Jallianwala Bagh stands as a memorial, its walls and narrowed exits still bearing witness. Reginald Dyer’s ten minutes of fire revealed how an empire, ruled by fear, could destroy the very consent it claimed.
